title: Effect of Annealing Treatment on Electrocatalytic Properties of Copper Electrodes toward Enhanced CO2 Reduction
abstract: CO2 reduction (CO2RR) into added-value chemicals is a key contribution to solve energetic and environmental issues. The performance of Cu-based electrodes towards CO2RR is strongly affected by pretreatments and presence of impurities, such as copper oxides. We evaluated the effect of different treatments, electropolishing (Cu-p), and annealing treatments under oxidizing (Cu-Air) and reducing (Cu-H2) conditions, on the performance of Cu electrodes designed for CO2RR. Characterizations revealed the presence of Cu2O and CuO layers on the surface of the Cu-Air electrode. All electrodes formed only HCOO ions as liquid-phase products, with yield of 480 mg L 1 of HCOO and Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 30% for the Cu-Air electrode and 25 mg L 1 with FE of 16%, and 26 mg L 1 with FE of 10% for the Cu-p and Cu-H2 electrodes, respectively. Overall, the HCOO concentration increased with an increasing KHCO3 concentration, while the FE increased up to 46%, due to insertion of CO2 into the electrical double layer, generating an intermediate specie prior to the electrochemical CO2RR. CO2RR tests performed on the Cu-Air and Cu-p electrodes under galvanostatic conditions showed HCOO FE of 32% and 16%, respectively. Therefore, the increasing local pH mechanism does not play a key role in the liquid-phase products of CO2RR. The activity of the Cu-Air electrode for CO2RR remained stable over 64 hours. It was proposed that Cu was the active site responsible for CO2RR. CO, C2H4, C2H6 and H2 were formed by gas-phase electrochemical CO2RR using the Cu-Air electrode, with total FE higher than 65%. We have uncovered the role played by the type of pre-treatment in the performance of Cubased electrodes on CO2RR and the reason for the increased electrocatalytic activity of oxidized Cu electrodes.

sections.text:
Osmando F. Lopes* and Hamilton Varela[a]
CO2 reduction (CO2RR) into added-value chemicals is a key contribution to solve energetic and environmental issues. The performance of Cu-based electrodes towards CO2RR is strongly affected by pretreatments and presence of impurities, such as copper oxides. We evaluated the effect of different treatments, electropolishing (Cu-p), and annealing treatments under oxidizing (Cu-Air) and reducing (Cu-H2) conditions, on the performance of Cu electrodes designed for CO2RR. Characterizations revealed the presence of Cu2O and CuO layers on the surface of the Cu-Air electrode. All electrodes formed only HCOO ions as liquid-phase products, with yield of 480 mg L 1 of HCOO and Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 30% for the Cu-Air electrode and 25 mg L 1 with FE of 16%, and 26 mg L 1 with FE of 10% for the Cu-p and Cu-H2 electrodes, respectively. Overall, the HCOO concentration increased with an increasing KHCO3 concentration, while the FE increased up to 46%, due to insertion of CO2 into the electrical double layer, generating an intermediate specie prior to the electrochemical CO2RR. CO2RR tests performed on the Cu-Air and Cu-p electrodes under galvanostatic conditions showed HCOO FE of 32% and 16%, respectively. Therefore, the increasing local pH mechanism does not play a key role in the liquid-phase products of CO2RR. The activity of the Cu-Air electrode for CO2RR remained stable over 64 hours. It was proposed that Cu1+ was the active site responsible for CO2RR. CO, C2H4, C2H6 and H2 were formed by gas-phase electrochemical CO2RR using the Cu-Air electrode, with total FE higher than 65%. We have uncovered the role played by the type of pre-treatment in the performance of Cubased electrodes on CO2RR and the reason for the increased electrocatalytic activity of oxidized Cu electrodes.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
The development of technologies to convert CO2 into addedvalue products (e.g. CO, CH4, C2H6, HCOOH, CH3OH) has been enormously considered as an alternative for climate change mitigation, besides the possibility of renewable energy production.[1–7] The electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to hydrocarbons using Cu-based electrodes has been particularly investigated,[8–10] though achieving higher efficiency, selectivity and stability is still in progress.[5,11–14] It has been reported that the Faradaic efficiency of CO2 reduction (CO2RR) is strongly affected by the pretreatment of the Cu electrode and the presence of copper oxide layers,[13,15–17] but their influences on the overall performance of Cu-based electrodes towards CO2RR are still not clearly established.[13,18,19]
Li et al.[16] tailored Cu-based electrodes by oxidizing annealing treatment followed by electrochemical reduction of the copper oxide layers formed onto the electrode surface. They found that the surface-modified electrode was more effective for CO2RR than the untreated Cu electrode, which was associated to the grain boundary structures resulting from electrochemical reduction of the suitably thick Cu2O layers.
Further studies on the CO reduction by nanocrystalline Cu prepared from reduction of Cu2O showed that the grain boundaries can be tailored by the oxide reduction treatment or nanocrystalline material preparation method in order to yield catalysts with higher activity and selectivity for long-chain products.[20] However, the performance of Cu-based electrodes having surface thick copper oxide layers on the CO2 reduction has not been properly evaluated yet.
Some authors reported that Cu-based electrodes with nanostructural surface morphologies display low-coordinated atoms as surface active sites for CO2 reduction.
[3,13] It has also been observed by experimental and theoretical studied that exposure of different Cu facets result in different activity and selectivity towards CO2RR.
[21–23] Sen et al. reported that the distribution of products and faradaic efficiency of copper nanofoam electrodes differ significantly from those obtained with smooth electropolished Cu electrodes. They attributed this difference to the high surface roughness, hierarchical porosity, and confinement of reactive species.[24] Further, the increase in local pH on the roughened electrode surfaces due to high current densities has been proposed as a way to change the reaction pathway.[17,25,26] Recently, Mistry and coauthors demonstrated that the roughness of oxide-derived Cu catalysts plays only a partial role in the catalytic performance, on the other hand, using operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy they demonstrated that the presence of Cu+ is a key factor for lowering the onset potential and enhancing the catalyst selectivity.[15] However, it has been assumed by several [a] Dr. O. authors that the Cu oxide layer is completely reduced over the CO2RR due to the relatively high potentials, thus the reduction occurs only on metallic Cu species.[27,28] Therefore, the increasing local pH effect due to surface roughness and the influence of the copper oxide layer on CO2RR by Cu electrodes must be investigated.
Formic acid is one of the most valuable CO2RR products, since it can be used as a building block for fine chemicals.[29] Moreover, formic acid can be used in low-temperature direct fuel cells, with higher efficiency than other C1 and C2 liquid alcohol fuels.[30–33] In this context, it is still necessary to develop catalysts with onset potential and current densities optimized for CO2RR. The electrode stability is another aspect of fundamental importance in electrocatalysis, since it is necessary that the catalysts exhibit high stability to be applied in several cycles or for long operation times.[12,28,34] Researchers have observed that despite bulk Cu electrodes are capable of reducing CO2 electrochemically in aqueous solution, their stability is insufficient for practical use.[34] In this sense, the low electrochemical stability of Cu electrodes must be overcome for practical purposes as catalysts for CO2 reduction.
[34] It has been demonstrated that the oxide passivation layer formed on the Cu film can reduce the onset potential for CO2RR as well as enhance the film stability.[15,16]
This work was aimed at studying the effect of CuO and Cu2O thick layer on the activity and selectivity of annealed Cu electrodes towards CO2 reduction to formic acid. To understand the effects of the thermal treatment and the Cu oxidation state, we compared the CO2RR efficiency of oxidized Cu electrodes with that of Cu electrodes annealed under reducing conditions. The main aspects (roughness, Cu oxide presence, electrolyte concentration, change in local pH) determining the enhancement of the overall Cu-based electrodes performance were evaluated. Finally, the long-term stability of the electrodes was investigated for several re-use cycles. The physico-chemical characterization of the electrodes was carried out before and after CO2RR.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Structural, morphological and electrochemical characterization of Cu-based electrodes
The Cu-based electrodes were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) for crystalline phase identification (Figure 1a). The XRD patterns of the Cu-p and Cu-H2 electrodes exhibited peaks assigned to cubic phase of pure metallic Cu (PDF: 05–0667), and no peaks related to impurities. On the other hand, the XRD pattern of the Cu-Air electrode exhibited peaks ascribed to metallic Cu and cubic Cu2O phase (PDF: 65–3288). The presence of Cu2O phase can be confirmed by the 2θ peak at ∼36.5. The Cu electrode surface was partially oxidized into Cu2O due to the annealing treatment at 500 °C under oxidizing condition (synthetic air). Visual inspection of the Cu-Air electrode revealed the formation of a black layer onto its surface, which suggests the formation of CuO.[35–37] The CuO phase was not verified in the by XRD pattern probably because
XRD is not sensitive to surface analysis.[38] Thus, it is suggested that the metallic Cu phase makes up the Cu-Air electrode bulk, the Cu2O phase is in the interlayer, while the CuO phase was formed as the upper layer.[39] This was confirmed by a grazing incidence angle X-ray diffraction measurement (Figure 1b). The presence of the following crystalline phases was observed: Cubic Cu (PDF: 05–0667), cubic Cu2O (PDF: 65–3288) and monoclinic CuO (PDF 45–0937)..
X-ray photoelectron spectrocospy (XPS) was used to investigate the chemical composition and the Cu oxidation state in the electrode surfaces. In fact, since electrocatalysis is a superficial/interfacial process, surface properties (chemical composition and environment) are more important than bulk properties.[40–42] The survey XPS spectrum (Figure 2a) of the Cup and Cu-Air electrodes exhibited Cu 3p, C 3 s, C 1 s, O 1 s and Cu 2p peaks, without any contamination. The C 1 s highresolution spectra of the Cu-p and Cu-Air electrodes (Figure 2b) showed the peak at 284.7 eV which corresponds to the sp2 C C bonds of the carbon standard used to calibrate the binding energies. The O 1 s high-resolution spectra (Figure 2c) showed the presence of oxygen in both electrodes. The Cu-p electrode

The surface morphology of the Cu-based electrodes was investigated via scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The SEM image of the Cu-p electrode (Figure 3a) revealed a smooth surface, as expected, since the electropolishing treatment was performed to obtain a featureless surface.[13,45] In the electropolishing, a certain amount of electrode material and impurities are removed from the electrode surface, while the rough parts are preferentially dissolved, thereby resulting in a smooth surface.[13,46] This phenomenon occurs because the terraces are stabilized by the formation of an ordered adsorbate layer, therefore the protruding parts on the electrode surface dissolve faster than the terraces.[47,48] The Cu-H2 electrode (Figure 3b) also exhibited a smooth surface, because the reducing annealing treatment does not involve any reaction able to change the electrode surface morphology. sections.heading: Electrochemical reduction of CO2 – Selectivity and Mechanism
sections.text:
To understand the performance of the Cu-based electrodes on CO2 reduction, cyclic voltammetry (CV) was performed in 0.1 M of KHCO3 saturated with argon or CO2 (Figure 6a). The CV curve of Cu-Air in argon exhibited a cathodic peak on the negativegoing sweep, which is due to reduction of Cu2O into metallic Cu starting at 0.27 V, while the H2 evolution was initiated at approximately 0.3 V. On the other hand, the CV curve of CuAir in CO2 exhibited a cathodic peak related to Cu2O reduction at low current density and shifted to lower potentials, i. e. 0.47 V. Further, it was observed that the H2 evolution and probably CO2 reduction initiated at approximately 0.25 V. It can be clearly observed that in CO2 the current density related to H2 evolution and/or CO2 reduction decreased when compared with the argon-saturated condition, indicating that CO2 interacted with the Cu electrode. [13,31,49]
Figure 6b compares the CV curves of the Cu-based electrodes. The electrochemical behaviors of the Cu-p and Cu-H2 electrodes were similar, both electrodes exhibited the same reduction onset potential, but the Cu-p electrode showed higher cathodic currents than Cu-H2. This comparable behavior was somewhat expected, since both electrodes exhibited similar properties, as observed by XRD and SEM. On the other hand, the Cu-Air electrode showed a lower onset potential and cathodic currents almost 4-fold higher than those of Cu-p and
Cu-H2. The increased cathodic current density obtained with the Cu-Air electrode could be attributed to its higher roughness, because the electrode exhibited a roughness factor approximately 9-fold larger than those of the Cu-p and Cu-H2 electrodes (Figure S2). This result corroborates with the SEM images.
It was not possible to assign the high cathodic current densities obtained with the Cu-Air electrode to the CO2 reduction, since this reaction occurs concomitantly with H2 evolution. To confirm the CO2 electroreduction performance, we conducted a chronoamperometry experiment at 0.65 V for 16 h (Figure S3).An aliquot was collected and analyzed by HPLC to verify the CO2RR products in liquid phase. The chromatogram proved that all electrodes generated only formate anions (HCOO ) as a liquid-phase CO2RR product (Table 1), confirming that all electrodes were active towards CO2RR. As observed in Table 1, the Cu-Air electrode produced 298 mg L 1 of HCOO , while the Cu-p and Cu-H2 electrode produced 25 and 26 mg L 1, respectively. Further, the Cu-Air electrode exhibited a Faradaic efficiency (FE) related to the CO2 to HCOO conversion of approximately 30%, while the Cu-p and Cu-H2 exhibited FE of 16% and 10%, respectively. noteworthy that the increased FE for the Cu-Air electrode cannot be directly related to its larger surface roughness, since the increase of roughness should result only in an increased amount of HCOO and not in an increase of selectivity and decrease of onset CO2 reduction potential. The oxidizing annealing treatment increased the Cu electrode electrocatalytic activity and FE towards CO2RR also probably due to the presence of different active species (Cu2O and CuO) at the electrode surface.
Some authors[21,23,50] have shown that there are two main routes for CO2 reduction, the main one is the adsorption of CO2 by the carbon atom to form CO, which is the intermediate chemical species in the formation of all CO2RR products (except formic acid). The second route proceeds via adsorption of CO2 by the oxygen atom, resulting only in formic acid generation. It has been observed that the CO2RR performed with pure metallic Cu electrode results only in trace amounts of formic acid,[13,50,51] so the fact that the Cu-Air electrode produces formic acid as the major CO2RR product indicates that there are other active sites involved in the electrocatalytical process, in this case the Cu2O and CuO phases.
A key parameter in electrocatalysis is the nature and the concentration of the electrolyte, being KHCO3 recognized as the best electrolyte for CO2 electroreduction. The effect of the KHCO3 concentration (0.1 to 0.7 M) in the CO2RR was also evaluated, and we observed that both onset potential and total current were KHCO3 concentration-dependent. The CV curve of the Cu-Air electrode for 0.7 M KHCO3 showed a low onset potential and a higher cathodic current density in comparison the curve registered with 0.1 M KHCO3, indicating that the CO2 reduction efficiency increased with the increasing KHCO3 concentration (Figure 7). This was confirmed by monitoring the reduction current at 0.65 V for 16 h and afterwards an aliquot was collected and analyzed by HPLC. The 0.5 M KHCO3 concentration showed the best performance in the HCOO formation in comparison with other conditions. It can be observed that the HCOO FE decreased when the KHCO3 concentration was increased above 0.5 M. This result could be explained by: (i) the insertion of CO2 into the electrical double layer between the adsorbed HCO3
and K+ ions, where the electrophilic carbon and the nucleophilic oxygen of CO2 interact with HCO3
and K+, respectively. The formation of new HCO3-C bonds results in the weakening of the C O bond, turning the CO2 into a more reactive molecule and facilitating the electron transfer from the Cu electrode to CO2. The injection of electrons happens through the HCO3-C bond, the electron-rich oxygen atom attracts a proton and the formate radical is formed.[52] Resasco et al. showed that HCO3 can be
considered as a relevant hydrogen donor for HCOO formation.[53] In this sense, the higher the electrolyte concentration the higher the hydrogen availability; (ii) high KHCO3 concentrations lead to high current density due to the increase in the electrolyte conductivity (the increase in KHCO3 concentration raised the conductivity from 9.9 to 38.5 mS cma 1). The increase in the current density hastens the consumption of CO2 molecules dissolved near the Cu-Air electrode surface, but CO2 exhibits a mass transport limitation, while the water reduction is not a mass transport-limited process.[5,17,54] Consequently, the increase in current density reduces the HCOO FE.
The enhancement in the overall performance of the oxidized Cu electrode has been attributed solely to the increase of surface roughness and consequent increase in current density,[17,25,26] as observed for the Cu-Air electrode in Figure S3). This process consumes H+ in solution due to H2 evolution, raising the local pH, which could alter the reaction pathway or selectivity for CO2 reduction. Gupta et al.
[25] modeled the local pH changes during the electrochemical CO2 reduction in KHCO3 solution. The local pH near the electrode surface during electrolysis was found to be higher than the bulk value and was dependent on the current density, electrolyte concentration, and stirring speed.[25] Kas et al.[26] observed that the product selectivity towards hydrocarbons formation was dependent on the oxide layer thickness due to local pH changes during electrolysis. The increased surface roughness and consequent increased current density of the Cu-based electrodes lead to an increase in the H+ consumption, due to H2 evolution, this phenomenon cause an increase in the local pH.
To evaluate the local pH effect, the CO2 reduction was performed under galvanostatic conditions (-5 mA.cm 2 for 16 h) with the Cu-Air and Cu-p electrodes (Figure S4), because it is expected that both electrodes can alter the local pH in a similar manner in this condition. It was observed that the CuAir and Cu-p electrodes produced 306 mg L 1 (FE of 32%) and 124 mg L 1 (FE of 14%) of HCOO , respectively. this is an indicative that the local pH effect does not play a pivotal role in

In this sense, the reason for the higher CO2 reduction rate exhibited by the Cu-Air electrode is most likely due to different active sites (CuO and Cu2O). Further, it can be observed that in the galvanostatic experiment (Figure S4) the Cu-Air electrode needed a potential of approximately 0.65 V to keep the current density at 5 mA.cm 2, while for the Cu-p electrode the necessary potential was approximately 0.95 V. Therefore, the Cu-Air electrode showed a higher production of HCOO and FE at a lower potential, i. e. lower power consumption. It can be concluded that the Cu-Air electrode is intrinsically superior to the Cu P electrode.
We also evaluated the local pH effect on the performance of the Cu-Air electrode for CO2 reduction using different cathodic current densities (-5, 10 and 20 mA.cm 2). In this case, it was expected that the higher current density the higher the local pH due to the faster H+ consumption. As depicted in Table 2, the Faradaic efficiency remained relatively unaffected
despite the change in the local pH. It is an indicative that the changes in local pH do not influence the performance and selectivity of the Cu-Air electrode for CO2 reduction to HCOO
. We observed that the enhancement in the CO2 reduction performance and selectivity with the increasing KHCO3 concentration occurred due to a low ohmic resistance (i. e. higher conductivity). Further, it was suggested that CO2 may be inserted into the electrical double layer in such a way that the HCO3
and K+ ions interacted with the electrophilic carbon and the nucleophilic oxygen of CO2, respectively, generating an intermediate specie prior to the CO2 electrochemical reduction.[52] This fact would explain the increase in the HCOO selective formation as a function of the KHCO3 concentration.
Evaluation of active surface and stability
It was verified that the presence of different active structures (i. e., Cu2O and CuO) was also responsible for the enhanced CO2 reduction performance exhibited by the Cu-Air electrode. This observation has been provided by several authors.[15,55,56] Nevertheless, it has been stated that the potentials applied for proper CO2 reduction are usually high enough to reduce CuO and Cu2O into metallic copper,
[16,17,20,57] which seems inconsistent with the results reported here. In this sense, it is necessary to study the electrocatalyst active surface, and evaluate the key parameter in the catalytic CO2 reduction process, i. e. the stability of the catalyst over several reuse cycles, since the
active structure may not be stable under the reaction conditions.
The Cu-Air electrode stability was evaluated in four reuse cycles, c.f. Figure 8. It can be observed that the Cu-Air electrode
was stable after 4 cycles (i. e. 64 h of operation), with no significant change in the HCOO yield and Faradaic efficiency. This is an important result since previous works reported that the stability of Cu-based electrodes is maintained only for 6 h of operation.[12,28] Moreover, this result is surprising because under such reaction conditions (at 0.65 V for 16 h) the CuO and Cu2O are not expected to be stable.
[16,17,20,57] The stability of the CuO and Cu2O phases under thermodynamically unfavorable conditions can be related to the highly roughened surfaces and low-coordinated sites that are formed after annealing treatment, which may bind more strongly to oxygen, favoring the stabilization of the oxides over the CO2RR. Additionally, the highly porous films formed onto the electrode might have also served as favorable oxygen reservoirs.[15] This results agree with conclusions from Cuenya et al.[15] In other words, the roughness is not the only feature responsible for the enhanced reactivity of the oxidized Cu electrode, because the copper oxide phases are likely to be stable and play a determining role in the electrode reactivity.
However, it can be observed that the current density reduced with the increasing number of cycles, being stabilized after 8 h of experiment. This is likely related to the H+ ions transport through the membrane (Nafion 117) used to separate the cathode and anode chambers,[58] additional studies in this regard are currently in progress.
XPS analysis (Figure 9) and SEM (Figure S7) characterizations were performed before and after CO2RR to understand the stability of the Cu-Air electrode and identify the active site determining on the reaction. The survey spectra of the Cu-Air electrode (Figure 9a) before and after CO2RR exhibit comparable peaks but with different intensities. The C 1 s peak intensity

This was confirmed by FTIR analysis (Figure S5) of Cu-Air electrode surface after the CO2 reduction experiment. It was observed the presence of an intense band at 1631 cm 1 assigned to the C=C bond stretching, which confirms the presence of carbonaceous species at the Cu-Air electrode surface.[59] It can also be verified in the C 1 s high resolution spectra (Figure 9b) that the C 1 s peak was more intense after CO2RR. The O 1 s high resolution spectra (Figure 9c) exhibit changes, i. e. a shift in the O 1 s peak due to partial reduction of CuO (529.8 eV) into Cu2O (531.4 eV). It can be observed that residual CuO and Cu2O phases remained stable even after CO2RR. The Cu 2p high resolution spectra (Figure 9d) exhibit slight changes due to partial reduction of CuO and Cu2O to Cu metallic, the peak at 933.9 eV was split into two peaks at 932.1 eV (related to metallic Cu) and 934.5 eV (related to Cu2+). Therefore, it is an indicative that residual CuO and Cu2O remained stable even after CO2RR.
Another indication that residual CuO and Cu2O remained stable over the CO2RR can be verified by the gridding XRD analysis (Figure S6) of Cu-Air and Cu-p electrodes after CO2
reduction. The intensity of the peaks related to CuO and Cu2O was substantially decreased after CO2 reduction. However, even after the CO2 reduction, the presence of the Cu oxide phases was observed. On the other hand, XRD pattern of the Cu-p electrode showed only peaks related to metallic Cu. Therefore, the Cu oxide phases identified in the Cu-Air electrode after CO2RR cannot be related solely to the rapid formation of native oxides upon removal from the reactor and exposure to air. Moreover, Mistry et al.[15] demonstrated that a layer of native Cu oxide with thickness lower than 3nm is formed onto reduced Cu electrodes upon air exposure. This explains why XRD analysis cannot be used to verify the presence of copper oxide phases.[15] Additionally, this result agrees with previous works, in which the stability of copper oxide phases over the CO2 reduction was observed.[15,55,60–62]

Bocarsly and co-workers evaluated the HCOO formation mechanism from CO2 reduction using oxidized metal electrodes using in situ attenuated total reflectance infrared (ATR-IR).[63,64] When In/InOx and Sn/SnOx were used as electrocatalysts for the CO2 reduction, they observed the formation of an intermediate metal-carbonate specie, which was subsequently converted to HCOO . On the other hand, when the bare metallic electrocatalyst was used there was no formation of metal-carbonate. In summary, it was demonstrated that the surface metal oxide was fundamental for metal-carbonate formation. Additionally, the formation of this intermediate was the key step in the HCOO formation. Therefore, based on the stability of the Cu eletrodes over CO2RR and the previous reports, it can be proposed that the formation of a surface-bound copper carbonate is a key step involved in the formation of HCOO from reduction of CO2 by Cu-based electrodes. The first step of this reaction is the two-electron reduction of the electrode from a native CuO to a Cu2+ oxyhydroxide (CuO + H2O ! Cu (OH)2). This specie can further reacts with CO2 to form the surface-bound carbonate. The carbonate formed at the electrode surface undergoes the necessary transfers of two electrons and one proton for formate generation, which quickly desorbs from the return Cu2+ oxyhydroxide surface.

sections.heading: Characterization of gas-phase products
sections.text:
We have focused so far on the CO2RR liquid-phase products (i. e. HCOO ), but some gaseous products could also be formed (i. e. CO, CH4, C2H6 and C2H4), in addition to hydrogen evolution. In this sense, the cathodic chamber of the electrochemical cell was connected in line with gas chromatography during the CO2RR under galvanostatic conditions (from 2.7 to 27.7 mA cm 2). It was verified the formation of the following products for all experimental conditions: H2, CO, C2H4 and C2H6, as can be observed in Figure 10. HCOO is the major CO2RR product, followed by C2H6, CO and C2H4, in other hand, the formation of H2 from water reduction showed a Faradaic efficiency higher than 30%. At low current densities (-2.7 and 5.5 mA.cm 2), the CO2RR Faradaic efficiency was higher in comparison with that of the side reaction. The FE of the C1 and C2 reduced products under these conditions were larger than 65%. The increase in the current density increased the Faradaic efficiency of the side reaction (H2 evolution) from 34% (at 2.7 mA.cm
2) to 62% (at 27.7 mA.cm 2). This is because the CO2 dissolved near the CuAir electrode surface is consumed faster at large current densities and the CO2 molecules exhibit mass transport limitation, while the water reduction does not exhibit this limitation.[5,17,54]

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, we demonstrated that oxidized Cu electrodes exhibit greater electrocatalytic activity and selectivity towards
the reduction of CO2 to HCOO . The key feature behind the improved Cu electrode performance was the higher electrochemical active surface area mainly composed of CuO and Cu2O phases. One possibility for the stabilization of Cu
+ under the high reductive conditions for CO2RR is the highly roughened surfaces with low-coordinated sites formed by oxidizing annealing treatment, which bind more strongly with oxygen, thereby stabilizing the oxides over the CO2 reduction process. Furthermore, the increase in local pH due to the high current densities reached on the highly roughened electrode surfaces was found to play a minor role in the Cu electrode electrocatalytic performance. The improvement on the performance and selectivity of the electrodes for CO2 reduction due to increase in the KHCO3 concentration occurred possibly due to insertion of CO2 into the electrical double layer, generating an intermediate specie prior to the CO2electrochemical reduction. The Cu-Air electrode was stable for 64 hours of operation, this occurred most likely because the residual CuO and Cu2O remained stable even after CO2RR. Finally, the Cu electrodes displayed Faradaic efficiency towards CO2 reduction higher than 65% under optimized conditions in comparison with side reactions.
Supporting Information Summary
The supporting information includes the detailed procedure to obtain the electrodes, the characterization parameters of the electrodes, and the evaluation of Cu-based electrodes performance on CO2 reduction. SEM image, roughness factor determination, cyclic voltammetry, chronoamperometry and galvanostatic experiment, FTIR and XRD analysis are also provided.
